c.v: The trick is that the heap is a

values. Once it has k of them, its smallest element is the weakest of the survivors, so the next reading either beats it and takes its place, or loses and is dropped. When the input runs out, the k largest are inside and the smallest of those is the k-th largest.

That is O(n log k) time, because each of the n readings does at most one push and one pop of a heap of size k, and O(k) extra space. The alternative answers are worth naming out loud. Sorting and indexing is O(n log n) time and changes or copies the input.

from the sorting topic is O(n) on average and the fastest of the three when you may rearrange the input and have it all in memory. The heap wins when n is much larger than k, when the readings arrive one at a time and you cannot hold them all, or when you want the whole top k rather than one element.
You pass with a size-k heap of the right polarity, the

guard on k, and O(n log k) and O(k) stated. A max-heap of all n elements popped k times is correct at O(n + k log n) and a partial pass, because it holds every reading. Sorting, or a heap of the wrong polarity that keeps the k smallest, is a fail.

where every parent compares at least as high as its children, index i's children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, its parent at (i − 1) / 2, with no pointer stored and no separate node. That single rule says nothing about siblings or cousins, so a heap is not sorted, and the one certain position is the root: whichever element compares highest under the chosen ordering.

The problem is repeatedly asking for the current largest, or smallest, element while the set keeps changing, without paying to keep everything else in order too. Sorting after every insertion, or scanning the whole collection for the extreme each time, does more work than the question needs; the invariant a heap keeps is exactly the part of sorting the question actually uses.

reads the root, O(1). A push appends the new element at the back and sifts it up, swapping with its parent while it outranks it, walking at most the tree's height, O(log n); a pop swaps the root with the last element, shrinks the range, and sifts that element down from the root, also O(log n). The tree is complete by construction, filled level by level with no gaps, so its height is always ⌊log₂ n⌋ whatever order elements arrived in, unlike a search tree's. Building a heap from a whole container at once costs only O(n), most elements sitting near the leaves with almost nothing to sift, cheaper than pushing them in one at a time.

and hides the rest: no iteration over the other pending elements, no erasing or re-prioritising one that is not on top, and no access to the container without going around the adaptor. Reach for a plain
and the heap algorithms once you need any of that, a scheduler that cancels a task rather than only running the next one.

The mistake that survives code review is the comparator's direction: the rule always means "less", but a sort places the least element at the front of the range while a heap places the greatest at the top, so

handed to a heap gives the smallest element first, the opposite of a sort with the same comparator. That reversal is the interview question in miniature: naming which spelling gives a min-heap, and why it reads backwards, before writing a line of code.

c.v: The tree is in the indices. Index 0 is the root, the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of index i is (i − 1) / 2, so a node reaches its children and its parent by arithmetic and no link is stored. That is the whole reason to prefer this shape to the

nodes of the search tree topic: one allocation for the whole structure instead of one per element, no child pointers to pay for or follow, no destructor recursion to overflow the stack, and a tree that is

by construction, every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right. Completeness means the height is always ⌊log₂ n⌋, whatever order the elements arrive in. The search tree's height was 4096 or 28 for the same 4096 keys depending on the insertion order; a heap has no such case.
The invariant is weaker than sorting, which is why it is cheaper. Every parent compares at least as high as its children, and that is all. Read the output above:

is a valid heap, and it is not sorted, and 4 sits above 8's subtree while being smaller than 8. Nothing is known about siblings or cousins. The one element whose position is certain is the root, and a heap is the right structure exactly when the root is all you ever ask for.

Building a heap has two costs, and which one you pay depends on how you build it:

c.v: stays under 3n = 12,288 comparisons on all three inputs, which is the O(n) bound: it sifts down from the last parent backwards, and most of the elements are leaves with no work to do, so the total is linear rather than n log n. Pushing one at a time is O(log n) per push and O(n log n) in the worst case, and the worst case is a run of increasing values, because each new element is the largest so far and sifts all the way to the root. That is the 40,974 comparisons in the first row, close to n·log₂ n = 49,152 and 6.68 times what
needed. Descending input is the other extreme: each new element stops at its parent immediately, 4,095 comparisons in total.

And notice which input made pushing expensive: values in increasing order, the same shape that turned the search tree into a chain and the textbook quicksort into O(n²). Sensor readings arrive in time order.
Three places in robot code want this structure.

: the next task to run is the one with the earliest deadline, which is the worked example. A

: a search that always expands the cheapest unexplored state next, which is what Dijkstra's algorithm and A\* are, and which the graph topic reaches. The intervals topic left a promise here too: the smallest number of meeting rooms is a min-heap of end times, where each meeting either reuses the room whose meeting ended earliest or opens a new one, and the heap's size is the answer.
A robot's scheduler holds tasks with deadlines and always runs the most urgent one. That is a min-heap by deadline, and a min-heap is the same code as a max-heap with the comparison turned around:

Equal values must come out in list order, so a 1 from list 0 precedes a 1 from list 1. Test three lists with a shared value, three lists where one is empty, three empty lists, a single list with a repeated value, and no lists at all. State the time and the extra space, and say what changes if the lists are so long that only one element of each fits in memory.
The heap holds one cursor per list, the element each list is currently offering. Take the smallest, write it out, and put back the next element of the list it came from:

blocks.text:
three lists       1 1 2 3 4 4 5 6
one empty         1 2 4 5 6
all empty         (none)
one list          2 2 7
no lists          (none)

c.v: Every element enters and leaves the heap once, and the heap never holds more than k cursors, so it is O(N log k) time and O(k) extra space beyond the result. Concatenating and sorting is O(N log N): for k = 4 and N = a million, log₂ k is 2 against log₂ N of 20, a factor of ten in comparisons.

Three details are worth defending. Empty lists are skipped at the start rather than tested in the loop, so the heap only ever holds a cursor that points at a real element. The tie-break on the list index is what makes the merge stable, the same rule the merge sort exercise used to take from the left half on equal values. And

is carried in the cursor rather than derived, because a cursor knows nothing about where it came from otherwise; storing an iterator instead works and ties the cursor's lifetime to the list, which is fine here and would not be if the lists could grow.

The last part of the question is why this shape exists. When each list is a file or a topic on the wire and only its front element is in memory, this algorithm does not change at all: the heap holds one element per source, and the rest stays where it is. That is an external merge, the same structure a rosbag merge or a log-file merge uses. For exactly two lists the heap is overkill, and
writes the merged result into an output range in O(N).
